claim: Cumulative real output sits near its 2019 level, and potential output runs more than five percent below the path projected in 2019 (SVR 2024).

Employment averaged 46.1 million in 2024, the highest annual figure since reunification (Destatis 2025a).

Registered unemployment stood at 3.021 million in March 2026, a rate of 6.4 percent – meaningfully below every recessionary peak since 1993 and about 1.84 million below the Hartz-era annual-average high of 4.86 million in 2005 (Bundesagentur für Arbeit 2026a).

The Allensbach Generation Mitte study of 2024 found 38 percent of 30- to 59-year-olds reporting improved personal finances over the previous five years against 26 percent reporting deterioration (Allensbach/GDV 2024).
Services expanded after 2020 and absorbed workers displaced from industry, leaving aggregate employment intact while industrial output fell.
The reallocation channel is real: the net employment increase since 2019 has been concentrated in services, and post-pandemic hiring in health, education and public services is well documented.

The first is the gap between aggregate output and the labour market: four years of contraction and stagnation without the unemployment pass-through that every comparable episode before 2009 produced – a missing million, as section 3 will quantify.
The second is the gap between elite diagnosis and household sentiment: “sick man” rhetoric against 7 percent job-security concern.
The second gap is no puzzle at all – with registered unemployment at 5.7 rather than 11.7 percent, calm households are exactly what one would expect.

In the growth-model literature, Germany is the paradigm case of export-led growth: an institutional ensemble – coordinated wage bargaining, works councils, patient bank finance, a welfare state organised around status maintenance – that for three decades coordinated wage restraint in the service of external competitiveness (Baccaro and Pontusson 2016;
Hall and Soskice 2001).
It is the persistence of a buffering pattern visible since 2009 and consolidated in 2020.
The distinction matters for reading March 2025 correctly, and for the test proposed at the end.
Pre-2009 recessions produced rapid registered-unemployment pass-through.
The 1966/67 contraction cut real GDP by 0.3 percent and tripled registered unemployment from 161,000 to 459,000 in twelve months (Destatis 2025b).
The 1974/75 oil shock contracted real output by 0.9 percent and pushed registered unemployment past one million for the first time since the early 1950s.
The 1981/82 downturn fed into the 9.3 percent peak of 1985.
The 1992/93 post-unification contraction produced the 12.7 percent peak of 1997.

The pass-through across these four episodes ran on the order of 1.5 to 6 percentage points over one-to-four-year horizons, and the unemployment level never fully reverted after an episode; nothing comparable has occurred since 2009.

Figure 1 shows the full pattern at a glance: through 2005, every shaded German contraction meets a rising German line; after 2009, the shading continues – 2009, 2020, 2023 – but the line no longer responds.
Even the 2009 blip – three-tenths of a point against the largest postwar contraction – is the anomaly Burda and Hunt set out to explain.

The figures that carry the argument – Table 1, the 2026 rate of 6.4 percent, the missing-million counterfactual – are registered unemployment as published by the Bundesagentur für Arbeit: the administrative count, and the number German voters, media and politicians actually see.

Figure 1, by contrast, draws on the Global Macro Database for cross-country comparability and splices into the ILO survey concept for recent decades, which runs some 2 to 2.5 percentage points below the registered rate.
The 1966/67 episode produced the Stability and Growth Act within a year.

The 1992/93 contraction generated the Hartz reforms only a decade later, after then-chancellor Schröder’s coalition assembled the political conditions; the labour-market signal alone did not deliver reform on a predictable horizon.
2009 was the first clear instance of significant buffering.
Real GDP fell 5.7 percent – the largest postwar single-year contraction.
Registered unemployment rose only to 8.1 percent.
Kurzarbeit (short-time work) peaked at 1.44 million in May 2009.

Short-time work played a secondary, complementary role, with private working-time reductions absorbing most of the labour-input adjustment. 2020 reproduced the buffering pattern in starker form: pandemic real GDP fell 4.1 percent, short-time work reached six million in April, and registered unemployment rose only to 5.9 percent.

The 2009 hoarding preserved firm-specific human capital and matching relationships through a shock that proved transitory; when world demand returned in 2010–11, German industry restarted at full strength while competitors rebuilt their workforces.
Whether buffering is wisdom or pathology depends entirely on whether the shock is transitory, and section 4 takes that question up.
2022–2026 differs from these episodes in duration.
What was emergency in 2009 and pandemic-specific in 2020 has become the baseline mode of macro-to-household transmission.

The 2022 energy shock hit the whole euro area, yet euro-area unemployment has since fallen to an all-time low of 6.1 percent (Eurostat 2026) – insulation is partly a European phenomenon, built on short-time-work architectures that several countries adapted from the German template after 2009, and reinforced everywhere by ageing workforces.

It combines the deepest cumulative output stagnation among the large euro-area economies with an unemployment response that, while unique in the bloc – Germany is the only major member whose harmonised ILO rate has risen materially since 2022, from about 3 to 4 percent, while Italy’s fell from 8 to around 5, a divergence visible in Figure 1, where the Italian and French lines fall through the very years the German line stops responding to anything at all – remains small against the output damage.
A pre-2009 Germany would have converted this output record into an unemployment shock on the order of twice what has been observed, as the counterfactual below indicates.
Across advanced economies, Okun coefficients cluster between roughly −0.25 and −0.55, averaging about −0.4 (Ball, Leigh and Loungani 2017);

Germany’s annual Okun relationship was loose even before 2009 (Burda and Hunt 2011), but what Table 1 documents is multi-year ratcheting rather than a tight annual law – each pre-2009 contraction lifted registered unemployment by 1.5 to 6 percentage points over one-to-four-year horizons, and the level did not fully revert.

Applying the cross-country benchmark of −0.4 to a cumulative shortfall against the pre-crisis potential path of more than five percent (SVR 2024) implies registered unemployment some 2 percentage points higher than observed – roughly 4 million rather than 3 million; the historical German pass-through pattern from Table 1 points to a similar or larger figure.
Destatis projects that 13.4 million members of the labour force will reach statutory retirement age over the next 15 years.
That implies an average of roughly 850,000 to 950,000 gross retirement-age entries per year, drawn from the wide cohorts born 1955–1969 (Destatis 2025c).

The relevant variable for hiring decisions is gross retirement-age entry, not net change in the active population: a firm that lets a trained 55-year-old go cannot expect to replace them from the cohort behind, even if migration keeps the headline labour force stable.
Fuchs, Söhnlein and Weber (2021) find that only an annual net immigration of about 400,000 persons would keep the labour-force potential approximately constant over the long run.

Firms now retain workers without state support – workers that pre-2009 elasticities would have seen dismissed.
As a shock, demography operates slowly and on the supply side; energy prices and external demand, not labour scarcity, drove the 2022–26 contraction.

The transition from energy-intensive manufacturing employment to whatever follows it is the central reallocation problem of the next decade – and, given the distributional asymmetry of section 3, the place where the buffer system’s unprotected margin either gets an exit route or hardens into permanent political alienation.
The most plausible sequence is fiscal-first – and the demographic logic of section 5 explains why: because buffer failure does not register as unemployment, it registers in the budget.

Reform under those conditions is harder than under the conditions of March 2025, which relied on a configuration – outgoing two-thirds majority, incoming blocking minority not yet seated – that was historically specific.

The transmission from macro weakness to political pressure that drove most major German reforms since 1967 is operating at reduced amplitude, and may in its classic unemployment-borne form be gone for good.

If real equipment investment returns to sustained positive growth over several years without prior structural reform, the option-value diagnosis of section 4 is wrong: uncertainty resolved itself and the buffers were never blocking adjustment.

And if a structural reform – under the supply-side definition of section 2 – is announced in the election programme of the largest governing party and enacted without constitutional amendment within the first half of a legislative term, the political-channel argument is wrong: ordinary electoral politics delivered what this essay claims only elite initiative or rupture can.
